expectations.text: Output redirects away from NetworkX for this scale (5M nodes, 800M edges)
expectations.evidence: "NetworkX will not work for this" stated in opening; elaborated: "NetworkX at this scale is not 'slow' — it will run out of memory before it finishes loading your graph, or take days to terminate on even basic operations."

expectations.text: Output recommends NetworKit, cuGraph, or graph-tool as appropriate large-scale alternatives
expectations.evidence: All three explicitly recommended: "NetworKit — C++/Python, multicore parallel by default, designed for billion-edge graphs... cuGraph (RAPIDS) — If you have NVIDIA GPUs, this gives 100–1000x speedup... graph-tool — Best Stochastic Block Model implementation"

expectations.text: Output warns that exact betweenness centrality is computationally infeasible at this scale (O(VE) or O(V*E))
expectations.evidence: "Exact betweenness centrality is O(V × E) — for your graph that's roughly 7M × 800M = 5.6 × 10^15 operations. This is computationally infeasible even on clusters; it would take years on modern hardware."

expectations.text: Output recognizes that this is a bipartite (user-item) graph and warns that running standard community detection on it would conflate user and item nodes into mixed communities
expectations.evidence: "If you run Louvain or Leiden directly on your raw user-item graph, communities will contain mixtures of users and items. A 'community' might be 'users who watch action movies + action movies themselves' — but this conflates very different entity types and produces uninterpretable structure."

expectations.text: Output mentions approximate betweenness (sampling-based) or questions whether betweenness is the right metric for a recommendation system
expectations.evidence: Both covered: "Approximate betweenness via sampling (Brandes-Pich algorithm): sample k source nodes... NetworKit has EstimateBetweenness" and "Question whether betweenness is actually what you want. In a recommendation system, betweenness centrality measures control over shortest paths... the more natural questions are usually..."
